cards.front: What should you know about cell division?
cards.back: is how organisms grow and repair damaged tissues. New cells are produced when existing cells divide. In humans, this happens constantly - for example, your skin cells divide every few hours to replace worn-out cells.

cards.front: What should you know about chromosomes?
cards.back: are structures in the nucleus that contain DNA (genetic material). Human body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Sex cells (gametes) have 23 chromosomes (one of each pair).

cards.front: What should you know about the cell cycle?
cards.back: is the series of stages a cell goes through to grow and divide. It has three main stages: growth, DNA replication, and mitosis.

cards.front: What should you know about stem cells?
cards.back: are undifferentiated cells - they have not yet specialised for a particular function. They can divide to produce more stem cells, or differentiate into specialised cells (like nerve cells, muscle cells, blood cells).

cards.front: What should you know about embryonic stem cells?
cards.back: can differentiate into ANY type of cell. This makes them very useful in medicine but also raises ethical concerns because the embryo is destroyed when stem cells are harvested.

cards.front: What should you know about adult stem cells?
cards.back: (e.g. from bone marrow) can only differentiate into a limited range of cells. They are less useful but have fewer ethical issues since the donor is not harmed.

cards.front: What should you know about therapeutic cloning?
cards.back: involves creating an embryo with the same DNA as the patient. Stem cells from this embryo would be a perfect genetic match, so the body would not reject them.

cards.front: What should you know about the main ethical issue?
cards.back: is about embryonic stem cells. To harvest them, the embryo is destroyed. Some people believe this is wrong because the embryo could have developed into a human being.

cards.front: What does Embryonic stem cells mean?
cards.back: Early-stage embryo (4-5 days old) (e.g. Any type of cell in the body (totipotent/pluripotent))

cards.front: What does Adult stem cells mean?
cards.back: Body tissues (e.g. bone marrow) (e.g. Limited range of cell types related to their tissue)

cards.front: What does Could cure many serious diseases mean?
cards.back: Embryo is destroyed - some see this as taking a potential life

cards.front: What does Improves quality of life for many people mean?
cards.back: Each embryo has the potential to become a human being

cards.front: What does Embryos used are often from IVF and would be destroyed anyway mean?
cards.back: Adult stem cells could be used instead (fewer ethical issues)
